# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has always been a fact of urban life, but climate change is turning what was once an inconvenience into a public health emergency. Cities are inherently hotter than their surroundings—the urban heat island effect can raise urban temperatures by several degrees Fahrenheit compared to nearby rural areas, and the difference is often largest at night, when bodies desperately need to cool down. Heat waves now kill more Americans annually than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and the deaths are not distributed randomly. They cluster in neighborhoods with few trees, lots of pavement, and aging housing stock. The question of how cities can make summer more bearable is therefore not merely a question of comfort. It is a question of equity, of urban design, and of whose suffering we consider acceptable. The good news is that cities have a substantial toolkit: trees, smarter street design, better housing, and expanded public transit all work. The complication is that each of these tools involves tradeoffs, and residents frequently disagree about which tradeoffs are worth making.
